items.title: Nightmare Eclipse Drops Windows Zero-Day Exploit ‘SignDrop’
items.summary: It abuses CLFS and Windows Defender to trigger arbitrary file creation in the context of the antimalware process. The post Nightmare Eclipse Drops Windows Zero-Day Exploit ‘SignDrop’ appeared first on SecurityWeek.
instructions: According to the security researcher, SignDrop has been tested on Windows 11 26H2, Windows 11 26H2 Experimental, and Windows Server 2025 Experimental, and should work on 80% of the world’s Windows installations. “You’re generally vulnerable if your Windows installation is older than 90 days,” Naceri says.
Last year, Microsoft introduced CLFS logfile authentication to mitigate exploitation, which relies on authentication codes to check file integrity.

A standard user can create a log file and specify a path to an associated container in it, and then coerce Windows Defender to open the file in the context of the antimalware engine by calling the signature update RPC interface.
SecurityWeek has emailed Microsoft for a statement on SignDrop and will update this article if the company responds.

items.title: Software Transparency Is Changing: Allan Friedman on SBOM, AI BOMs and What Comes Next
items.summary: SBOM pioneer Allan Friedman joined the SecurityWeek Podcast to discuss why knowing what is inside software is only the beginning, how AI is complicating software supply chain visibility, and what organizations should be doing with SBOM data once they have it. The post Software Transparency Is Changing: Allan Friedman…
instructions: SBOM Is About Response, Not Just Inventory Much of the early SBOM conversation focused on whether vendors could generate the documents and whether customers should require them.
The objective, however, should ultimately be deeper integration.

Transparency Should Favor the Defender Resistance to SBOM adoption has often centered on concerns about intellectual property and the possibility that providing detailed information about software components could benefit attackers.

Organizations should be able to understand what their systems depend on, correlate that information with emerging threats and vulnerabilities, determine where actual exposure exists and make risk decisions quickly enough to matter.

items.summary: CVE-2026-19868 can let attackers holding credentials for a different login method get past SAML checks, including SAML-enforced MFA. The post SonicWall Patches Exploited SonicOS Vulnerability That Weakens VPN Logins appeared first on SecurityWeek.
instructions: SonicOS versions 7.3.4-7013 and 8.2.3-8015 resolve the issue, and there are no workarounds. “Customers are strongly urged to upgrade to the latest release as soon as possible to mitigate the associated risks,” SonicWall said.

It’s one of seven vulnerabilities described in an advisory published on November 6. “An authentication enforcement vulnerability in SonicOS SSLVPN service may allow a user with valid credentials for an alternate authentication method to bypass SAML authentication controls.
Under Binding Operational Directive 26-04, federal agencies must address it by November 20.
